title: 还能读吗
intro: 这一期围着注意力转：书还在不在、误读怎么发生、谁还肯把一件事读完。默认先看一类；要看整期，点最后的「全部」。

articles.title: The End of Reading Is Here
articles.summary: 霍罗威奇写后阅读时代：识字还在，书却没了；特朗普是第一个后文字总统。
articles.briefing:
Rose Horowitch's Atlantic cover story is this issue's keystone, and it should be read as a historical argument rather than as a lament from a magazine that sells subscriptions. The print headline is colder than the online one: "The Age of Reading Is Over." Optimists once treated universal literacy as a destination the species was walking toward. Horowitch's claim is that the destination was a short anomaly. People still consume text — emails, captions, threads, the sludge of a phone — but the desire to sit with a book-length work is dying across cohorts, and the next generation is arriving with even less of it. The higher-order skills that books trained, comprehension and synthesis over hours rather than seconds, do not automatically transfer to a feed. You can be literate and postliterate at once. That is the weather she is describing.

The opening move is Alexandrian on purpose. Ptolemy wanted a library that would hold the world's writing. Ships were ransacked for scrolls. Euclid may have studied there. The legend is useful because it names a bet: that a civilisation could store its mind in text and that later minds would still want to open it. Horowitch's present is the inverse bet. We have more stored text than any library could have imagined, and less patience for the form that made the storage matter. The article is not saying that people have forgotten how to decode letters. It is saying that the long form — the thing a weekly digest exists to defend — is losing the contest for attention, and that the loss is not a vibe. It is a change in what a public can still do together.

Donald Trump appears as a representative, not as a mascot. Horowitch calls him the first postliterate president: difficult to imagine as the leader of a country whose information still moved primarily through text. He pioneered a style that exploits a distracted, disputatious age. The sentence is easy to cheer or hiss. Keep it as a diagnostic. A politics organised around clips, insults, and the next notification does not need a reader. It needs a reactor. AI, in the piece, is not a sidebar. It is an accelerant. If a model can summarise, draft, and flatter, the already-weak habit of finishing a book has one more excuse to die. Things, she writes, are about to get worse, and fast.

It may seem self-serving for a writer at a 169-year-old magazine to carry a torch for reading. Horowitch admits the interest. The admission does not cancel the claim. The people who lose in a postliterate age are not only novelists. They are anyone whose work requires holding a long argument in mind: a statute, a scientific paper, a history that will not fit a slide. A university reader should feel the piece as a description of the room they are already sitting in. You can still read. The question is whether the surrounding culture will keep paying you to.

This issue keeps returning to that question. Snow and Leavis fought over what kind of mind a country should trust. Zarin rereads Lessing and finds bowls that were never on the page. Walt Hunter wants the blue book back because a chatbot can mimic a five-paragraph essay and cannot mimic a hand under a clock. Horowitch is the door they all walk through. If the age of reading is over, a digest is either a relic or a refusal. Read her when you have a sitting. The Atlantic's job is the full walk, including the parts a briefing would only flatten. This one is here so the argument is already in the room: literacy without books is a different civilisation, and it has already begun.

articles.title: Culture clash
articles.summary: 斯诺的「两种文化」不是文理分科小品：德莱瑟重读他与利维斯的对骂，争的是对生活取什么态度。
articles.briefing:
Sam Dresser's Aeon essay asks you to stop using "the two cultures" as a dinner-party shrug about scientists who do not read Dickens. C. P. Snow's 1959 Rede Lecture at Cambridge coined a phrase that outlived him and then forgot him. The remembered version is bland: sciences here, humanities there, a gulf, a plea for more conversation. The lecture Snow actually gave was a manifesto. He had been a physicist and became a novelist of bureaucratic ambition. He told the Senate House that literary intellectuals were natural Luddites, that industrialisation was the only hope of the poor, and that scientists had "the future in their bones." He considered research a moral act. He wanted power moved toward men who could raise a standard of living. He later became a baron. He expected a Nobel. He did not get one, and he blamed, among others, F. R. Leavis.

Leavis's 1962 Richmond Lecture is one of the great academic assassinations. He called Snow an intellectual nullity, a man who thought of himself as a novelist and did not begin to exist as one. The hall emptied in outrage. The Spectator printed the text with cruel caricatures of Snow's face. Dresser is not here to referee manners. He wants the temperament under the insult. Leavis named the system that had crowned Snow "technologico-Benthamism": a stance that treats analysis, utility, and correct answers as the royal road to wellbeing. Snow reduced life to a standard of living. For Leavis, that was already a crime against what literature is for. "Life," in his criticism, is not a definition. It is what great writing makes present, and if you ask him to define it you have already left the room. Terry Eagleton later mocked the mysticism. Dresser asks you to take the mysticism seriously as a disposition: some minds want the mystery left unblemished; some want it solved.

The politics of the two men overlapped more than the legend allows. Both were meritocratic liberals, hostile to egalitarian fashion, proud Englishmen. Lionel Trilling said that if ever two men were committed to England, Home, and Duty, they were Leavis and Snow. The fight was not Labour versus Tory. It was Bentham versus Coleridge, fact versus meaning, future versus past. Snow's scientists were "steadily heterosexual" in a line that now reads as a period joke and was then a claim about seriousness. Leavis's "life" was an elite pedagogy: a caste of readers who would keep the highest culture and dispense judgment. Both positions are easy to parody. Dresser's useful stubbornness is to keep the pair as temperaments rather than as a problem with a third-culture solution. John Brockman's later "third culture" is mentioned and left on the shelf.

Read this after Horowitch. She says the book is dying. Dresser says the fight about what a mind is for did not die with the book. A postliterate public will still have Snows and Leavises. They will just have less text in common. Snow wanted scientists in the corridors of power. Leavis wanted a reader who could answer "This is so, isn't it?" with "Yes, but — ." The but is the humanities. The corridors are still there. The question this week keeps asking is whether anyone will still do the reading that makes the but possible. Dresser's essay is long because the original quarrel was long. This briefing is the cut. The original is where Snow's modest tone and Leavis's froth have to sit in the same room.

Read Aeon. The argument is already in the room: the two cultures were never only about syllabi. They were about whether life is a problem to be improved or a mystery to be undergone.

articles.title: Blue Bowls
articles.summary: 扎林重读《金色笔记》：记了五十年的蓝碗并不在书里；误读本身就是这部小说教的事。
articles.briefing:
Cynthia Zarin's Harper's essay begins with a doll and a mistake, which is the right order for a piece about rereading. A matryoshka sits on her desk: stories inside stories, hard to reassemble once taken apart. She has gone back to Doris Lessing's The Golden Notebook, a book that mattered to her at sixteen and stayed in her mind as a talisman. What stayed, she thought, were images: two women in a London flat, swans, strawberries eaten from blue bowls, four notebooks packed inside a novel. Fifty years later she searches the opening and finds the strawberries. She does not find the bowls. The cobalt she had lived with was her own invention. She bought blue bowls for her kitchen anyway. The prototypes of those bowls are the ones she imagined. A break in the fourth wall, she calls it, like a plaque to a fictional character on a real bridge.

The novel's architecture is the other matryoshka. Free Women is a conventional story about Anna Wulf and Molly, divorced, raising children, done with the Communist Party. Inside it sit four colour-coded notebooks: black for Rhodesia and the wartime novel Anna is ashamed of; red for the Party; yellow for a novel-within-the-novel about an affair that is also Anna's; blue for a diary. Lessing said Anna separated things from fear of chaos. Zarin, in a season of bad news, had remembered the book as a manual for compartmentalising. Rereading, she finds she missed central lessons and invented others. Irony had not yet stained the lintel when she was sixteen. She did not know that "Free Women" was meant as a joke. What drew her then was the friendship: two women alone, a definite article teaching a girl how grammar assigns value. Friendships between girls barely existed in the books she had. Elizabeth and Charlotte revolve around marriage. Jo's plot is Laurie. Anna and Molly were something else.

The 2012 Guardian symposium on the book's fiftieth birthday is in the piece because it has to be. Margaret Drabble remembered blistering honesty and was troubled by Lessing's "real man," the homophobia, the women who still made all the tea. Zarin asks a new small circle to read along. Her youngest daughter lasts fifty pages: "Communism is bad. And?" A friend sends a photo of the paperback on its side: "Nope." The book that organised conversations among women about work and desire now meets a generation that will not sit with it. That fact belongs in a week whose cover story is the end of reading. Zarin is not scolding the daughter. She is watching a talisman fail to travel.

Lessing's biography is not decoration. Persia, Rhodesia, a mother who would not pick up a crying child, two marriages, two children left, Peter taken to London with the manuscript of The Grass Is Singing. Jenny Diski lived next door with a door cut in the wall that was always left open. Coetzee wrote that Lessing knew the nineteenth-century novel was exhausted. 1962, the year of publication, is listed as a newsreel: Sartre's apartment bombed, Eichmann hanged, Marilyn dead, the Cuban missiles still months away. Zarin is not doing trivia. She is placing a book that tried to hold chaos in four colours next to a year that would not be held.

Misreading is the method, not the accident. You carry a book for fifty years and the bowls are yours. Horowitch says we are losing the long form. Zarin shows what the long form does when you return: it corrects you, and it lets the correction become part of the life. Read Harper's when you have a sitting. This briefing will not restage The Golden Notebook. It will say what kind of essay you are opening: a rereading that admits the most vivid object was never there, and that the admission is the point.

articles.title: How we meet the future
articles.summary: 拉尔斯顿拿拉姆齐的「迎接未来」重审刻板印象：概括不是罪，罪在把人只当成一类。
articles.briefing:
Tom Ralston's essay won Aeon's first Philosophy Prize, which is a reason to read it and not a reason to treat it as a sermon. The question in the title is the load-bearing wall. If we could not generalise, the world's complexity would paralyse us. Does that ever excuse stereotyping? A child who has only known a golden retriever will approach an XL Bully. A person who met one rude Brit will call the nation rude. We condemn the second as a moral failure and sometimes as a sign of low cognitive ability. We hear less about undergeneralising, because almost no one is at risk of it. Ralston's cut is that the desire to generalise is not the mistake. The mistake is what we do with a tool we cannot live without.

The intellectual ancestor is Frank Ramsey, dead at twenty-six, notes found by Richard Braithwaite in 1930. Ramsey asked what it means to believe that all humans are mortal. Not, he decided, an infinite conjunction of particular facts. A belief in a generalisation is a habit, a disposition: you treat the next human you meet as mortal. Those habits are "the system with which we meet the future." Two people can agree on every past death and still disagree about whether all humans are mortal, if one of them is a techno-utopian who thinks immortality is in principle available. The disagreement is about the disposition's future applications, not about the archive. That is why Ramsey asked what a generalisation is for, not only what would make it true.

Generic generalisations — "cats are furry," without "all" — are the everyday form. They tolerate exceptions. They do not demand a precise proportion. Sarah-Jane Leslie's mosquito example is in the piece: people will accept that mosquitoes carry West Nile even when they know that one percent do. The same features that make generics useful are the hallmarks of stereotypes. A universal is easy to kill with one counterexample. A generic survives a crowd of them. Stereotypes, Ralston says, are part of how we meet the social future. They impose structure. We do not revise them every time we meet an exception, for fear of losing the structure.

None of this is a permission slip. Stereotypes built from bad evidence — film, police practice, the stop-and-search numbers in Britain — systematically misread ambiguous cases. They harm because they refuse to see a person as a person. Kahneman and Tversky's heuristics are the psychological rhyme: Linda the bank teller, the conjunction fallacy, representativeness. A mind that never used a shortcut would drown. A mind that never revises a stereotype is not using a shortcut. It is refusing the world. Popper's advice, which Ralston takes as a start rather than a finish, is to hunt counterexamples. A single immortal would kill "all humans are mortal." Social life is rarely that clean. The tension the essay will not dissolve is the one it names at the outset: a cognitive obligation to simplify, a moral obligation to treat people in their specificity.

This issue is about attention. Horowitch says we no longer finish books. Ralston says we never finished people: we meet them as members of a class because that is how a finite mind arrives. The adult move is not to pretend you have no generics. It is to know when a generic has become a sin. Read the original. The prize essay is longer than a digest can be, and the Ramsey pages are the part a summary would flatten. This briefing is here so the tension is already in the room.
Popper is only a start because social generics are not laboratory universals. You will not meet a single counterexample that kills "women are X" in the way an immortal would kill mortality. Ralston knows this, which is why the essay's last movement is about seeking disconfirming lives without pretending that one life falsifies a habit. The XL Bully ban is in the opening for a reason. A state that generalises about a breed is doing what a mind does, at scale, with a statute. Whether that statute is wise is a different question from whether generalising is a sin. The prize essay's discipline is to keep those questions from collapsing. A digest that flattened them into "stereotypes are useful, actually" would be doing the thing the piece refuses. Read him as a philosopher who will not let the moral conclusion write the epistemology in advance.

articles.title: Thucydides the perspicacious
articles.summary: 修昔底德不是「强权即公理」的祖师：波兰斯基与席林格写，他揭的是强者与弱者都会自欺。
articles.briefing:
It is almost never a good sign when Thucydides is in the news. David Polansky and Daniel Schillinger open there, and they are right to. The historian of the Peloponnesian War is usually summoned either to announce that great-power conflict is returning, or to license the strong to do what they can. Mark Carney quoted the Melian line at Davos as a critique of American behaviour under Trump. Others quote it as a permission. The essay's claim is that both uses should be disappointed. Thucydides writes to expose the delusions of the strong and the weak, the unjust and the just. Self-deception is the leitmotif. Because it is perennial, the book remains timely in the way he said it would.

The famous sentence is already a little false in English. "The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must" is more ominous than the Greek. A closer rendering: those who are superior do what they can, and the weak yield. The Athenians are not saying that might makes right. They are saying that the language of justice has a place among relative equals, and that Melos is not an equal. They invite the Melians to drop pretences. The Melian oligarchs refuse, trust the gods and the Spartans, and are destroyed: the men killed, the women and children enslaved. Within six months Athens launches for Sicily and loses a force the size of a city. Many readers want Sicily to be punishment for Melos. Thucydides, in one of his rare direct statements, declines to blame the war's outcome on any single encounter, including Sicily, or even on the pursuit of empire. Every city rules to the limits of its power. The question is whether it does so without illusions.

The Spartans are the other self-deception. They call themselves liberators of Hellas and vote for war less because the allies persuaded them than because they feared Athenian growth. They butcher sailors, raze Plataea, annihilate Hysiae, and invite two thousand of their bravest helots forward with a promise of freedom before making them disappear. Their passion for justice, the authors write, has grown into a taste for punishment. They receive a fraction of the attention paid to Melos because they committed atrocities without Athenian rhetorical flourishes. The Athenians, who talk as if they have no illusions, overestimate reason. They insist on a dialogue they cannot win. They want not only conquest but the satisfaction of hearing their worldview acknowledged. Silent conquest would have been cheaper. In Sicily they vote for glory and then put cautious Nicias in charge, as if his temperament could cancel their aim.

Hobbes, the first to translate Thucydides from Greek to English, praised a writer who does not digress to lecture. That reserve is why every generation can impose a reading. Realism, a twentieth-century word Nietzsche was early to apply here, is available in the text and is not the whole text. E. H. Carr wanted realism as a corrective to utopianism. Kant wanted perpetual peace. Thucydides wanted a possession for all time, which is a different ambition from a policy brief. Carney's "middle powers" talk, the authors note, was vague on actual capacities. Announcements of American decline as cosmic punishment are wish-casting for a just universe. Faux-realism excludes the speaker from the logic of his own claims.

Read this next to Horowitch and Ralston. One says we have stopped reading. One says we meet the future with generics. This one says states meet the future with stories about themselves, and the stories kill. The original will take you through the plague, the exile, the quarries of Syracuse, the unburied. This briefing is the stance: do not quote Melos as a slogan. Quote it as a scene in which everyone is already lying to himself.

articles.title: The neverending house
articles.summary: 阿劳斯在圣地亚哥边缘看了二十年自建房：房子从不完工，家就在添砖加瓦里发生。
articles.briefing:
Consuelo Araos's essay is a housing piece that refuses to stay a housing piece. UN-Habitat's number is the one that will travel: more than 2.8 billion people, about thirty-five percent of the planet, lack adequate housing. Engels named the Housing Question in 1872 as a structural fact of industrial capitalism. For a century, rich states answered with public building, mortgages, the dream of mass ownership. The answer is failing in the capitals that invented it. Araos's wager is that the cities where the state-led paradigm never fully took hold — Latin America, Africa, Asia — still know something the policy paper has forgotten. Behind every housing problem is a dwelling problem. Behind the house as asset is the bond between building and living. In self-building, that bond is still visible.

Victoria is the person who makes the thesis walk. She worked in Araos's family home. The house was her favourite subject. Araos has been returning to it since 2007. Victoria ran from a foster family in a village of seaweed gatherers, barely went to school, had her first child before fifteen, six children in all, a disabled son already in his forties, a great-grandmother before fifty. Four generations under one roof, rooms rearranged, new ones added in the backyard and on top. She spoke in quantities: a sack of cement, two sheets of zinc, ten bars for a gate. They were "closing" the plot, "lining" the wooden walls, "raising" the kitchen floor, dreaming of "finishing" the bathroom in proper material — brick and cement, not wood, which did not count as solid. The processes were long, discontinuous, paused and resumed. A daughter who moved out after three decades still said the only place to go if her husband told her to leave was her mother's. The doors had never closed. The same house could also close in: crowded, no room to fight for your life. Victoria still wanted the terrace, the garden, the raised floor she never had space to finish.

Pliability is the keyword. A self-built house holds conflict open. A room might still be added. A definitive house, bought finished, forecloses the wager. Santiago's pericentral belt took shape from the 1960s through the 1980s by occupation and later regularisation. A quarter to a third of urban Latin Americans have lived in informal conditions as cities grew. These neighbourhoods were assembled by hand over generations. Araos is not romanticising precarity. She is refusing the technical illusion that a house is an object the state or the market can deliver complete. Dwelling is a verb that keeps happening.

The essay belongs in a week about unfinished attention. A book you do not finish is one kind of neverending. A house you cannot finish is another. Both are ways of living with something that will not resolve on a deadline. Horowitch's postliterate reader wants a summary. Victoria wanted another layer of cement. Read Araos for the fieldwork, the words that changed meaning, the moral expectation that children can always come home. This briefing is the door: the housing crisis is real, and the people who built their own cities already knew that a house is not a product. It is a life that keeps adding rooms.
Engels is in the essay so that the reader does not mistake fieldwork for a lifestyle feature. The Housing Question was never only about square metres. It was about who may occupy the city. Araos's twenty years on Santiago's margins are a long answer to a short policy sentence. Formalisation, when it comes, often arrives as a title that freezes a house that had been a process. A finished legal object can be sold, leveraged, inherited as an asset. Victoria's unfinished bathroom cannot. That is why the piece belongs next to Mishra and next to Horowitch. One is about a continent that outsourced its purpose. One is about a public that outsourced its attention. Araos is about households that never outsourced the making of a room. The UN number will get the summit. The sack of cement is the argument. If you only remember the 2.8 billion, you have read a press release. If you remember "lining" the walls, you have begun to dwell.

articles.title: All She Dreamed
articles.summary: 彭曼写爱丽丝·科特兰：丈夫死后坠入深渊，出来时带着更狂的梦，音乐至今仍像超前。
articles.briefing:
Ian Penman's Harper's piece is a review that behaves like a portrait, which is the right behaviour for Alice Coltrane. The occasion is the first full-length biography. The subject is a pianist and harpist who was already a musician before she was a widow, and who became something the jazz press still does not have a single word for. After John Coltrane's death she went into an abyss and came out not chastened but haloed with larger dreams. The records that followed — A Monastic Trio among them — take on sitar, tamboura, a spirituality that is easy to file as costume and harder to sit with. Penman's own favourite is Huntington, split with Ron Carter's double bass and Rashied Ali: serious music that is also quietly psychedelic. He reports, with the embarrassment of a man who knows how it sounds, that listening over days produced side effects. A soft blue light. A feeling of being centered. Colourful clothes. An abundance that reminded him of Sun Ra, of George Clinton, of a spirit world that does not ask your permission.

Alice's visions, recorded in her self-published Divine Revelations, are not a sidebar. Inside an Egyptian pyramid, Jesus arrives to the sound of a harp and presents a crystal scarab that vibrates with the strings. Penman's point is that her life is as odd and oneiric as the visions. Things happen and she accepts them as her due. Worlds open and she steps in, like a child into a first piano lesson. She goes to Paris and is daunted by nothing. Bud Powell, he suggests, was her first real guru, and perhaps the most elemental. The love of her life is taken and she lowers into pain and emerges with more dream, not less. The later life as Turiyasangitananda, the ashram, the monastic turn: these are not a retirement from music. They are the music continuing under another name.

A digest should not pretend to have heard every record. It should say what kind of person the piece is offering. Alice Coltrane is often introduced as John's widow, which is a true fact and a bad category. Penman writes against the category without needing to shout. The music still feels ahead of its time, which is a reviewer's phrase that here means something specific: it has not been absorbed into the playlist of what jazz is supposed to have been. You can use it as yoga incense. You can also let it rearrange a room. This issue's other lives — Patel in a remade Mecca, Hite on a motorcycle with surveys, Wes Brown on a mat after a father's death — are people who went into a practice and came out altered. Coltrane is the one who made the alteration audible.

Read Harper's for Penman's ear and for the biography's facts, which a briefing will not inventory. The argument is already in the room: grief did not shrink her. It gave her a larger instrument.
The biography's job, which Penman will not let a digest steal, is to keep the Cleveland and Detroit years from becoming a prelude. Alice McLeod was already a working musician, already in conversation with bebop, already a person with a sound, before the name Coltrane attached. The ashram years are often told as a vanishing. Penman tells them as a continuation: the harp, the organ, the chant, the students, a life that refused the industry's idea of a second act. You do not have to share the scarab vision. You do have to decide whether you will hear the later records as a widow's consolation or as a body of work. This issue keeps asking who is still listened to. Hite vanished after fifty million copies. Coltrane never had that kind of market and somehow remained more audible, if you know where to look. The looking is the biography's wager. Read Harper's for the records you have not put on, and for the refusal to make grief the only plot.

articles.title: Mecca and the mall
articles.summary: 帕特尔去麦加求精神续命：除了克尔白，她预期会看见的几乎都没了，门外是 Sephora。
articles.briefing:
Azania Imtiaz Patel went to Mecca in Ramadan 2026 to catch a break from a life of applications, first dates, and a laptop that would not yield a sentence. She was approaching thirty and felt the noose of squandered potential. A Quranic line she prays often is Moses in need of whatever good is sent down. She wanted a spiritual sugar rush that would let her stand up in the secular world. The umrah gave her renewed worship. The break from the ordinary never came. The essay is the record of that failure, which is also a record of a city.

Ihram is the consecrated state: no sex, no hunting, no cutting hair or nails, unstitched cloth for men, unadorned garments for women. Victor and Edith Turner's communitas is the anthropological name for the temporary equality. Pilgrims are guests of God, not of the kingdom, and on paper prince and pauper are alike. The shuttle's ticker said Welcome Guests of Ar Rahman. Then the mosque: oudh and rosewater, eyes on the marble because the first glance at the Kaaba is said to grant a prayer, swallows, drones, guards, and a black cube that is still, somehow, the only thing you can look at. Eliade's axis mundi is not decoration here. Mecca is the mother city. The Kaaba orients prayer and burial. Patel occupied, for a few hours, an imagined Mecca of prophets and mothers. Accessing it required her to suspend disbelief, because the complex around the cube is a $26.6 billion expansion, 1.564 million square metres, escalators, ramps, and a golf-cart track at 300 riyals. Lady Evelyn Cobbold, in 1934, prayed that the motor would never displace the camel. The carts now zip through the mosque itself.

Except for the Kaaba, the historically significant structures have been modified or destroyed. Safa and Marwa are an air-conditioned enclosure. Zamzam is taps. An eighteenth-century citadel came down for the Clock Tower complex, part mall, part hotel, a Big Ben that throws its shadow on the black cloth. Abu Bakr's house is a Hilton. Muhammad's birthplace is a library. Wahhabism supplies the ideology: tear down the graves and houses lest they become idols. The petrodollar supplies the glass. Ziauddin Sardar called it a steel-and-glass heaven of consumerism in the name of extinguishing idol worship. Irfan al-Alawi called it the Manhattanisation of Mecca. Patel steps out of ihram, snips a few curls, and finds Joe & The Juice, Sephora, Dunkin', Times Square billboards. The whiplash is the essay.

She will not presume to know what God thinks of today's Mecca. Cities evolve. Belief outruns anachronism. The unease, she decides, may be where ritual still lives. If all the world were holy, we would not need a navel. Those before us battled drought and death. We battle excess. 1.68 million foreign pilgrims had permits for that Ramadan; Muhammad's last pilgrimage was said to have thirty thousand. Infrastructure is not optional. Erasure is a choice. This issue's theme is what we can still read in a place. Patel went looking for a text she had been given as a child and found a renovation. Read Aeon for the smell, the shuttle, the grief that the floors are not the ones the forebears walked. This briefing is here so you know the piece is not a tourist complaint. It is a pilgrim admitting that the sacred now has to work against a mall.
Communitas is a fragile achievement, and Patel is honest about how much of it still happens: the chant on the walk, the white cloth, the fact that a prince is supposed to be a guest like anyone else. The essay's grief is not that the crowd is large. It is that the kingdom has chosen which past may remain. A mosque that can hold more bodies is a logistical mercy. A skyline that replaces the first caliph with a hotel is a theology. Wahhabism and the petrodollar are not the same force, and she does not mash them. One fears a grave becoming an idol. The other needs a clock tower that can be seen from the cube. Together they produce a sacred that must compete with Sephora. A reader who wants only a rant about Gulf kitsch will be disappointed. A reader who has watched a hometown museum become a mall will recognise the unease. The Kaaba is still there. That is why the shadow of the clock is a metaphor she almost apologises for, and then uses anyway.

articles.title: A second sexual revolution
articles.summary: 坎贝尔写海特：她是第一个大规模问女人感觉如何的人；五千万册之后，人和书都几乎被忘了。
articles.briefing:
In 1972 Shere Hite, a Playboy model turned feminist researcher, got on a motorcycle in a lace gown and handed surveys to women in Manhattan. Fifty-eight questions: what an orgasm feels like; whether you feel free to do what you want; whether sex is political. The answers became The Hite Report (1976), fifty million copies, still among the most-read books of the twentieth century, the thirtieth bestseller of all time. Rosa Campbell's Aeon essay is about a woman who asked women how they felt instead of telling them what to feel, and about how that woman and that book have largely vanished.

The first sexual revolution had already happened, if you count acts. Premarital sex among young American women had gone from a rarity to a majority. Ten million were on the Pill. California had no-fault divorce. What Hite found was more sex, not better sex. A little kiss, a little feel, he's on top, wham it's over. Male orgasm ended the event. The Joy of Sex still treated penis-in-vagina as the pièce de résistance. Women reported they had lost the right to say no: if you declined, you were lectured about being free. Hite's path into the movement ran through an Olivetti ad that used her face under the caption that the typewriter was so smart she didn't have to be. NOW marched. She joined consciousness-raising and noticed that women would talk about housework and ageing and not about sex. A weekend conference was too much. The anonymous questionnaire went instead: 100,000 copies, church newsletters, Brides, Mademoiselle, and Oui, a porn magazine, "in the interest of better communication."

The intellectual enemy was not only the bedroom script. It was Freud, still, and the neo-Freudians who had sent women to therapy for failing to have a vaginal orgasm. The clitoris was childish masculinity; the vagina was maturity; inability was neurosis. Women in the survey used therapeutic language to scold themselves. Hite, with Friedan, Firestone, Millett, wanted the time and money spent blaming themselves back. Kinsey had mapped frequency. Masters and Johnson had watched nearly ten thousand acts, concluded that female orgasm was clitoral, and then declined to dethrone penetration, because their values were monogamous and heterosexual — they ran a conversion programme for gay men into the 1970s. Hite's innovation was to bring feminism to sexology. Sex is sexist, she said in 1977: women's sex lives reflect a second-class position, as wages did.

Campbell is careful about the limits. Race went unanalysed. Black women and a Chinese American woman wrote back anyway and pushed the project further. Consent politics and girl-boss assertiveness later took a piece of Hite's advice — ask for what you want, specifically — and left behind her structural point: inequality is in the room before anyone says yes. Hite was combative, walked out of interviews, and is now a ghost in a culture that thinks it has finished her work because sex toys may yet appear in Westminster.

A person, in this week's sense, is someone whose questions outlive the brand. Hite asked, and the asking changed the available speech, and then the speech forgot the asker. Read Campbell for the motorcycle, the questionnaire, the Freud, the fifty million, the vanishing. This briefing is the door: the second revolution was listening, and listening is still the part that does not stay famous.
Campbell's closing movement is about what happened after the listening. Consent became the official language of good sex, which is a legal and ethical gain and also a narrowing. If the only question is whether a yes was clear, the older Hite question — would you like things to be different, structurally — can sound ungrateful. Girl-boss feminism told women to ask, specifically, in bed and at work. Hite had said that too. She had also said that the asking happens inside a wage gap and a script. The vanishing of the book is therefore not only a fame cycle. It is a political convenience. A culture that has absorbed the questionnaire's easiest advice can retire the woman who wanted the harder half. Fifty million copies and a ghost: that is a data point about reading as well as about sex. Horowitch says we do not finish books. Hite's book was finished by millions and then unfinished by memory. Read Campbell to put the motorcycle back in the story.

articles.title: The European Question
articles.summary: 米什拉问：大西洋共同体枯了之后，欧洲还能否提出一种不被美国决定的目的，而不只是牢骚。
articles.briefing:
Pankaj Mishra's Easy Chair is filed here as 经济 because it is about a political economy of dependence: who pays for security, who owns the intellectual weather, who still takes the post-politics job in Washington, Wall Street, or Silicon Valley. The occasion is the brutal reconfiguration of Europe and America under Trump — mockery of NATO, threats to abandon Ukraine, the costs of a war on Iran loaded onto weak European economies. Anti-Americanism is surging. Macron's strategic autonomy, Sánchez's talk of a European army and of China, Merz blaming German woes on a war he first endorsed, AfD and La France Insoumise calling to leave NATO, a Biennale boycott, seventy-five percent of Europeans viewing the United States more negatively than China. The question is whether continental powers can articulate a purpose not determined by decades of American cover.

Mishra's method is historical humiliation. William Maxwell's Americans weep at the French shore in 1948 and then notice that talk of Nazis slides into talk of Americans. Saul Bellow concluded that the French hated us. After 1945 the United States folded cultural ambition into geopolitical interest, pulled Mann, Arendt, Fermi, Einstein, and made New York the new avant-garde. Partisan Review announced that America had become the protector of Western civilisation. Thomas Mann wrote in horror that Europe was being treated as a colony and a strategic outpost. Coca-Colonisation met a mix of craving and shame. Sartre and Enzensberger kept a tradition of refusal alive; Pinter was perhaps its last bold voice, and even he, in the Nobel lecture, sounded like a man describing a successful hypnosis.

The post-1989 conversion was worse than the old hatred. Eastern Europe and, for a time, Russia performed Americanophilia as a rejection of communism, until shock therapy taught another lesson. Britain supplied wise Greeks to naïve Romans: Hitchens, Ferguson, a verbal facility that Gombrich distrusted. Rushdie wrapped in a flag. BHL giving American democracy a clean bill. Mishra remembers his own first visits in the 1990s, bemused by the infatuation, his view of the United States overdetermined by Asia — 1971, Nixon and Kissinger, the rehearsal for a president who talks of wiping out a civilisation. Today Europeans discover that Trump, Hegseth, Musk, Altman, and Karp may be Ortega's primitive men without the camouflage of inventions. A rupture still looks unlikely. Merz is a former BlackRock man who will not send his children to study in America and will not forgo the class's remunerative afterlife. Starmer sealed a Palantir contract after a meeting arranged by an ambassador who was also a shareholder in a Palantir lobbyist. A European army, Mishra writes, looks like a golden opportunity for American arms manufacturers. The most stalwart moral defence of Europe's peace commitment now comes from an American in the Vatican.

Valéry asked whether Europe would become a little promontory on Asia or remain the pearl of the sphere. Nietzsche wanted good Europeans. Weil wanted the continent to abjure empire. Judt wanted social democracy back. The present leaders, Mishra says, resemble human pinstripes. The intellectual deficit is the economic fact: a ruling class that cannot think without an American mirror will keep buying American systems and calling it strategy. Read Harper's. This briefing is the invoice: autonomy that still banks in New York is not autonomy. It is a subscription.
Nietzsche's good European, Valéry's pearl, Weil's refusal of empire, Judt's social democracy: Mishra lists them not as a reading list but as a measure of the present vacancy. The op-ed pages still speak of values. The leaders he names do not look like a brain trust. The more damaging claim is about incentives. A European politician who spends a career performing Atlantic loyalty can expect a fellowship, a board, a contract, a child at an American university. Trump humiliates the performance and does not cancel the aftermarket. That is why Merz can sour on sending his children and still be a former BlackRock man. That is why a European army can be announced in the same season as a Palantir signature. Dependence here is not only NATO's Article 5. It is a labour market for elites. Read the piece as political economy. The culture war about America is the surface. The invoice is the essay.

articles.title: China’s trade gap is narrowing. And other surprises
articles.summary: 二季度增长 4.3%，是 2022 年以来最弱；经济学人说，世界第二大经济体正跌进财政紧缩。
articles.briefing:
China's GDP figures are often suspiciously smooth. Last year the target was five percent and the $19 trillion economy grew by just that, as if 760 million workers and 30 million firms could be choreographed by a committee. This year Beijing allowed itself half a point of drama: 4.5 to 5. Few expected the official outcome to wander far. The second-quarter number, released on 15 July, therefore raised eyebrows. Growth was 4.3 percent year on year: not a disaster, slower than expected, the weakest since 2022, when cities were still being locked down for covid. The Economist's finance piece is a short, cold walk through what that number is hiding, and why a narrowing trade gap is not the comfort a surplus-hawk might want.

The magazine's habit, which this briefing will copy, is not to invent a secret percentage. The argument is structural. A state that has lived on exports, property, and local-government investment is trying to look disciplined while demand at home stays soft. Fiscal austerity, in this register, is not a German virtue. It is what happens when the old engines cannot be restarted at the old volume and the new ones — advanced manufacturing, the AI-adjacent export boom — do not employ or enrich enough households to replace the property machine. A trade gap that narrows can mean partners are buying less, or China is buying more, or both. It can also mean the surplus that unnerved the world is being trimmed by weakness rather than by a conversion to consumption. The piece's job is to keep those readings in view without treating 4.3 as a morality play.

Readers who want a collapse narrative will find the ingredients: property hangover, local debt, youth unemployment, a growth target that now has a range because a single number had become a joke. Readers who want a triumph narrative will find other ingredients: exports that, even as the headline cools, still ride global demand for the hardware of other countries' AI build-out. The Economist is not going to give you either hymn. It will give you a second-largest economy stumbling into a tighter fiscal stance while the rest of the world still prices China as a factory, a threat, and a market, often in the same sentence.

This issue's other economic pieces are about dependence (Mishra's Europe) and about a sport that cannot decide whether its golden age is a business. China is the factory those stories still run through. A Europe that talks autonomy still buys. A tennis tour that talks global still plays in a world whose second economy just printed its slowest non-lockdown quarter in years. Read the original for the tables and the tone. This briefing is here so you do not walk in expecting a crash or a miracle. You are walking in on a number that was not supposed to be allowed to look like a number.
A narrowing gap can be spun as rebalancing: more imports, a responsible surplus, a step toward the consumption story Beijing has promised for a decade. The Economist's suspicion, which the July number feeds, is that some of the narrowing is simply a weaker machine. If exports cool because the world is full or angry, and imports do not surge because households are still saving against a property ghost, you get a tidier external account and a worse internal one. Local governments that once paved their way out of a slowdown are refinancing rather than building. Youth who cannot find the jobs the old model advertised are not a footnote to 4.3. They are the political risk that a smooth GDP series is designed to hide. Read the original for the regional breakdowns this digest will not fake. Then decide whether you think the surprise is the miss, or the fact that a miss was allowed to appear at all.

articles.title: Can Tennis Survive Its New Golden Age?
articles.summary: 费德勒哭着离场之后，阿尔卡拉斯与辛纳已经把大满贯重新填满；莱文问：场上够炫，场下这门生意稳吗。
articles.briefing:
Josh Levin's Atlantic feature is a sports story filed as 经济 because the question in the title is not whether the tennis is good. It is whether the enterprise can survive the thing it asked for. The old golden age ended in tears: Federer sobbing at the 2022 Laver Cup, Nadal beside him, Serena writing in Vogue that she felt no happiness as she "evolved away" from the game. The roster behind them looked like a rebuilding year — Tsitsipas, Auger-Aliassime, Fritz without majors; Raducanu and Osaka out in the first round of that US Open. Fans were told to be patient. They did not have to be. That same fortnight, nineteen-year-old Carlos Alcaraz and twenty-one-year-old Jannik Sinner played five hours and fifteen minutes, a behind-the-back forehand, a saved match point, shot-making Levin calls extraterrestrial, the last ball at 2:50 a.m. The next night Iga Świątek and Aryna Sabalenka met in a Slam for the first time. Before the tournament the quartet had two majors, both Świątek's. Less than four years later they have twenty-one: seven Alcaraz, six Świątek, four each for Sinner and Sabalenka. Only Djokovic, still at thirty-nine, and Coco Gauff have taken more than one major in the same span.

On court, then, the product is astonishing. Off court, Levin says, they are not entirely happy. The print headline is "Tennis's New Golden Age." The online question is survival. A golden age in a professional sport is a labour market, a calendar, a television contract, a body that has to last, a public that has to care about rivalries that have not had twenty years to ripen. Federer–Nadal–Djokovic was a business because it was also a soap opera with three decades of episodes. Alcaraz–Sinner can be as beautiful and still be fragile if the tour, the slams, and the off-court economy cannot turn beauty into a durable institution. The piece, working in the orbit of Matthew Futterman's reporting on the cruelest game, is about stressors: the shape of a crisis that can arrive while the highlights are still going up.

Do not ask this briefing for a fake revenue table. The argument does not need one. It needs the structure: a sport that wept for its gods, received four new ones almost immediately, and is now asking whether greatness at this density is sustainable for the people who have to live inside it. Mishra's Europe is a dependence story. China's 4.3 percent is a growth story that looks like discipline. Tennis is a luxury export that still has to pay its workers in wear. Read the Atlantic when you have a sitting. The magazine's job is the players, the tears, the 2:50 a.m. ball. This briefing is here so the business question is already in the room: a golden age can be a cash register and a warning at once.
A golden age is also a calendar problem. The slams want nights that end at 2:50 a.m. because the product is drama. Bodies want sleep. Broadcasters want rivalries that can be sold in more than one language. Alcaraz and Sinner can supply the shots. They cannot, by themselves, supply the twenty-year story that made Federer a global brand. Świątek and Sabalenka have been doing the same work on the other side of the net, with less of the myth-making machinery that still prefers a men's narrative. Levin's question about survival includes that asymmetry. If the off-court unhappiness is burnout, the business response will be more exhibitions and more miles. If it is a deeper refusal — a generation that does not want to become a walking corporation — the tour will have to decide whether greatness is a job you can quit. Read the Atlantic for the matches. Keep the invoice in mind: astonishing tennis is not the same as a stable industry.

articles.title: How much of our existence do we owe to sugar?
articles.summary: 布兰德-米勒在《科学》上论证：糖在人类演化里是中心角色，早期或有三分之二能量来自甜食。
articles.briefing:
Jackie Flynn Mogensen's Scientific American piece is short and should stay the size of its claim. In 2017, a study of more than 140 primate species found that fruit-eaters had larger brains, on average, than peers who ate meat or leaves. Jennie Brand-Miller, emeritus at Sydney, called it a light-bulb moment. The brain runs on glucose. Perhaps sugary food had a hand in making us. The new analysis, in Science, models the mix of sugars, protein, fibre, starch, and fat across roughly four million years, from Australopithecus afarensis — Lucy — to modern foraging communities. Early hominins, the authors argue, may have taken as much as sixty-six percent of their energy from sweet foods, fruit and honey. Across the span, twenty to thirty-five percent. "No matter what period of human evolution, sugars were playing an important role."

Brand-Miller is careful, and the briefing will copy the care. This is not a licence to call the ancestors candy-eaters, and it is not a dismissal of meat. "Two parallel stories," she says: a balanced diet still needs protein, fat, and carbohydrate. Matt Sponheimer, at Colorado, who was not on the paper, grants the work value as conceptual space and then says the ground is uncertain. The authors assume Lucy ate rather like a chimpanzee. Fossil evidence, he notes, could point toward primates that eat very different foods. Almost no serious student of hominin diet thinks they were carnivores; the friendly fight is about proportions. The Paleo fantasy of a meat-rich past is the popular idea this paper is quietly walking past.

Brand-Miller wants a present implication. Humans cannot make vitamin C. We have sweetness receptors in the small intestine. We like the taste, and the liking did not come from a marketing department. Sweetness, she says, is something important to humans, and the desire should be satisfied on a regular basis. That sentence will be abused by anyone selling a bar. Keep it next to Sponheimer's caution. A model of deep time is not a menu.

This issue's science cluster is about what we can still see: sugar in the fossil diet, whirlpools on the sun, every animal Joel Sartore can still photograph. Horowitch says we have stopped reading long arguments. A Science paper about fruit is a long argument disguised as a sweet headline. Read Scientific American for the numbers and the dissent. This briefing is here so you do not walk out with a Palaeolithic doughnut. You walk out with a claim about energy, a warning about assumptions, and a reminder that the brain you are using to finish this paragraph is a glucose organ with a history.
The 2017 primate paper is the hinge, and it is worth keeping distinct from the Science model. Larger brains among fruit-eaters could mean sugar, or it could mean the spatial memory and planning that fruiting trees demand. Brand-Miller heard glucose. A sceptical reader can hear foraging. The new paper tries to quantify a diet no one sampled, which is why Sponheimer's "uncertain ground" is the adult sentence in the room. Assumptions about Lucy are not a scandal. They are the condition of the work. The scandal would be to treat the sixty-six percent as a measurement rather than a modelled ceiling. Popular nutrition will not observe the distinction. A digest for a university reader should. Sweetness as an evolutionary inheritance can sit beside a supermarket that industrialised it. The paper is about deep time. The abuse will be about dessert. Read Scientific American to hear Brand-Miller and Sponheimer in the same piece, which is the only honest way to carry the claim.

articles.title: Spectacular images reveal never-before-seen whirlpools on the sun
articles.summary: 夏威夷因努伊望远镜拍到日面等离子体涡旋：开尔文-亥姆霍兹不稳定性，可能是空间天气的引擎。
articles.briefing:
What does a star look like? Lee Billings's question is simple and the photosphere is not. We have had a crude map: granules a thousand kilometres across, lanes of cooling plasma, sunspots where magnetic fields flatten the boil, flares that can hit spacecraft and grids. The map showed hurricanes and missed the weather that makes them. The Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Hawaii — four metres, the largest and best solar telescope — has now resolved the edges of individual magnetic elements. They are not smooth. They are swirling. The images, checked against simulations and published in Nature, show whirlpools from about twenty to nearly two hundred kilometres across. Friedrich Wöger says the feat is like seeing ants on Earth from a hundred miles up.

The physics has a name the essay is right not to mystify. Kelvin–Helmholtz instability: two fluids sliding past each other at different speeds, shear, vortices like cream in coffee or a cresting wave. Theorists have speculated for decades that KHI in the photosphere could mix magnetised and unmagnetised plasma, braid field lines, store energy, and release it when the lines snap — flares, jets, space weather, and perhaps a piece of the coronal heating problem, the fact that the sun's outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than the surface we see. David Kuridze: observational solar physics has always been the story of resolving magnetic elements. For the first time the boundaries are not a blur. Mihalis Mathioudakis, not on the paper, calls it a breakthrough that will stand because it is imaging, not only a model.

Wöger is excited and then scientific: looking like a duck is not enough. The team compared DKIST's pictures with numerical slices of the photosphere and found the models reproduced the numbers and the dynamics. Further observations will hunt the vortices across wider stretches. Improved models will ask whether they are in fact the missing link in flux braiding. The discovery is one piece of a larger picture: how the sun works, and how its weather becomes ours.

A week about attention can use a telescope. The Inouye is a machine for refusing the postcard sun. Horowitch's reader wants a summary of the star. The star, at this resolution, is all edge. Read Scientific American for the images, which a digest should not pretend to replace. This briefing is the map: the photosphere is not a smooth lamp. It is a shear, and the shear may be why Earth sometimes loses a satellite.
The coronal heating problem is the romance that will tempt a headline, and Billings is right to keep it as a maybe. Flux braiding is a leading idea, not a closed case. What is not a maybe is the resolution: individual magnetic boundaries, Kelvin–Helmholtz vortices, a telescope that can finally see the shear theorists needed. Space weather is the civic reason to care. A flare is not a metaphor. It is a risk to a grid and a constellation of satellites. DKIST's gift is to make the engine less mythical. Granules and sunspots were the poster. The lanes between them, where plasma of different speeds pass, may be where the energy is braided. Further sweeps across the disk will say whether the first sunspot's edge was typical. Until then, the Nature paper is a local, stubborn fact. Read the original for the images. This briefing is only the physics in prose: the sun has weather at the scale of a city, and we have just photographed the gusts. Kuridze's line about the history of the field is the one to keep: solar physics has always been a race to resolve magnetic structure. Each generation's telescope made the previous map look coarse. DKIST is that race's present winner, not its end. If the vortices are common, textbooks will change. If they are a sunspot-edge specialty, the paper is still a local triumph. Either way, the postcard sun is finished.

articles.title: Photographer Joel Sartore’s quest to reveal every animal on Earth
articles.summary: 萨托尔拍了二十年、一万八千种：Photo Ark 是在物种消失之前，把它们一张一张存进方舟。
articles.briefing:
Twenty years ago Joel Sartore set out to photograph every species in human care. National Geographic's feature marks the anniversary of the Photo Ark: more than 18,000 creatures, a studio practice that treats a toad and a tiger as equal sitters, a conservation project that has to move faster than extinction. Sartore works out of Lincoln, Nebraska. The comparison to Noah is in the piece and is useful if you keep it secular. Noah did not favour the pretty. Neither does Sartore. The job is to gather the splendid and the unsightly before the list shortens. Shortly after 2026 began, the core team left for three weeks in Australia, Alice Springs to a lab in Hobart, 135 locations asked, 36 visited, the 18,000th species crossed somewhere in the sprint. Which animal was the landmark? He is not sure it matters. He will put a thumb on the scale to give attention to a species whose existence might depend on a portrait.

The scientific claim of the Ark is not that a photograph saves a habitat. It is that a public that has never seen a species will not fight for it, and that zoos and labs are the last places many of these animals can still be lit, posed, and looked at. Some of the 18,000 have already disappeared. Others are sliding. The portraits are a record and a recruitment tool. They are also an aesthetic: black background or white, the animal meeting the lens as a face. That aesthetic can be accused of making a studio out of the end of the world. The feature's better instinct is to stay with the pace. A man in a hurry, a team logging species, a conservation mission that has never been more urgent because the clock did not pause for the anniversary.

This issue keeps asking what we can still attend to. Sartore's answer is: one animal at a time, under lights, before the cage is empty. Horowitch says we do not finish books. Sartore is trying to finish a catalogue that cannot be finished, because the world is still producing losses. Read National Geographic for the pictures, which are the argument. This briefing will not restage a studio. It will say what kind of science this is: taxonomy as a public act, photography as a holding action, a Nebraska operation against a planetary thinning.
Sartore's studio rule — every species a face, no hierarchy of charisma — is an ethic and a trick. The trick is that a public will look at a beetle if the beetle is lit like a dignitary. The ethic is that the beetle was already a dignitary. Zoos and labs are compromised arks: captivity, politics, the smell of a backup plan. They are also, for many species, the last place a portrait can be made. The Australia sprint, 36 of 135, is the method in miniature. You ask everyone. You go where the door opens. You do not wait for a perfect wilderness. Critics will say the Ark aestheticises the end. They are not entirely wrong. A black backdrop is a choice that removes habitat, which is the thing actually dying. Sartore's reply, implicit in twenty years of repetition, is that a public that has never seen the face will not fund the habitat. Whether that reply is enough is the live question. Read National Geographic and look. The looking is the science here, for better and worse. Twenty years is long enough for a project to become a brand, and Sartore is not above the brand. He will stage a sitting to save a species that needs a poster. The honesty of that thumb on the scale is part of why the Ark still feels like fieldwork rather than a campaign. A Noah who admits he is lobbying is easier to trust than a Noah who claims to be only counting.

articles.title: Is AI ruining our skills? Early results are in—and they’re not good
articles.summary: 内镜医生用了人工智能，关掉它以后腺瘤检出率从 28.4% 掉到 22.4%；工程师用助手，概念测验更差。
articles.briefing:
Mariana Lenharo's piece, from Nature and reprinted in Scientific American, is the unromantic AI story of the week. Seventy percent of nurses and seventy-seven percent of physicians in a recent American survey worry about losing skills to over-reliance. The worry now has studies. In Poland, endoscopists who had each done at least 2,000 colonoscopies were given an AI that flags adenomas in real time, available some days and not others. Before the tool, they found at least one adenoma in 28.4 percent of exams. After they had been using it, their unassisted rate fell to 22.4 percent. The Lancet Gastroenterology paper suggests that even experts get worse at the job when the job has a prosthetic. Yuichi Mori, a co-author at Oslo, says there is no established fix. It should be a hot topic for a decade. Robert Wachter's gloss is that continuous exposure can make clinicians less motivated, less focused, less responsible when the system is off.

The software trial is smaller and, if anything, ruder. Anthropic ran a randomised test with fifty-two engineers on a basic coding task. All could search the web. Half were prompted to use an AI assistant. Afterwards, a quiz: the AI group averaged 50 percent, the others 67, and the AI group did especially badly on diagnosing errors. They had produced code without learning the concepts. Kevin Crowston, at Syracuse, names the disconnect: high performance, borrowed skill, no development. Tapani Rinta-Kahila, who a decade ago watched accountants forget routine tasks after ten years with a non-AI system, argues that generative models are the first technology to automate faculties long treated as uniquely human — thinking and interpretation. GPS eroded navigation. This erodes the thing you thought was you. Next generations of programmers may not understand foundations they never had to touch. The same, he says, for law and accounting.

The advice in the piece is not a ban. It is vigilance: know how much you are offloading, know the limits, do not trust output without a fight. Crowston hopes that naming the phenomenon provokes a choice about which skills to keep. Horowitch says we have stopped reading books. Hunter, next, wants handwriting back because a chatbot can do the essay. This study says the professional version of the same loss is already measurable in a colon and in a quiz. Read the original for the numbers and the caution that more work is needed. This briefing is here so the word deskilling does not stay a mood. It is a detection rate and a test score.
Rinta-Kahila's accountants are the unglamorous ancestor. A non-AI system, used for a decade, was enough to erase routine competence when the system went away. Generative models raise the same pattern from bookkeeping to interpretation. The Polish endoscopists were not novices. Two thousand colonoscopies is a career. The drop from 28.4 to 22.4 is therefore not a story about students cheating on homework. It is a story about experts becoming slightly worse at the thing they are still licensed to do. Mori wants more studies. He should get them. In the meantime, hospitals will keep buying the tool because the assisted days look better, and the unassisted days will be the ones a digest remembers. Crowston's hope — that naming the phenomenon provokes a choice — assumes professionals still have a choice. Many will not. The assistant will be policy. Read Nature via Scientific American, then decide which of your own skills you are already borrowing. Wachter has written a book on AI in medicine; his presence in the piece is a reminder that the field already has a literature, not only a scare. The scare is still earned. A detection rate that falls when the helper is off is a clinical fact. A quiz score that falls when the helper was on is an educational one. Together they describe a profession that can look more competent while becoming less so.

articles.title: What Students Learn From Blue-Book Exams
articles.summary: 亨特为蓝皮簿辩护：防作弊是表面，真正的好处是逼你在钟声里想；普林斯顿的荣誉誓约已经扛不住了。
articles.briefing:
Walt Hunter's Atlantic essay is the classroom rhyme to Horowitch's cover and Lenharo's deskilling. The blue book — sky-blue cover, red margins, two staples, NAME SUBJECT CLASS SECTION — had begun to disappear by the time he became a professor in 2013. Covid finished the job for many courses. Capstones, take-homes, portfolios felt more humane than Gradgrind. Locked browsers and honour codes were supposed to keep the take-home honest. A 2020 survey already had 62 percent of undergraduates admitting some form of cheating. Then the chatbot arrived. Princeton, after 133 years, gave up on its honour code and voted to proctor exams for the first time since the Gilded Age. Rose Horowitch, Hunter's colleague, reported that death. Sales of blue books are up as much as 80 percent at some universities since 2023. The unlikely hero is a pamphlet.

Hunter will not let the story stop at policing. Cheating is the occasion. Thinking on the page is the case. A five-paragraph essay with a thesis and evidence is a template any agent can mimic. A blue book is an athletic hour: the clock, the broken pencil, the walk to fetch a second book, the sentence that arrives in the margin as time expires. "Education is the single greatest thing Thoreau believes in," a student sneaks onto the edge of an American-literature final. A Morrison essay ends on the inside back cover: a good life is what we make it — now all we have to do is live it. The marks are indelible. Erasures stay. The booklet is a record of first thoughts. When we eliminate the possibility of writing badly, Hunter says, we eliminate writing's greatest satisfaction: watching our own words fall into order with only study and wits.

He knows the advocacy can look like old Professor Sophocles burning exams in 1857 to protest Harvard's move from oral to written. He does not care. The humanities, on his account, are not a fact-delivery system. They are habits: nimbleness, the ability to connect, the willingness to stand behind a commitment under pressure. Those habits are honed by writing into uncertainty. AI's promise — that removing craft lets students polish ideas — is a ruse. To see what a student has learned, look at the struggle to begin, and then at the moment the struggle is transcended. That is the full force of a mind taking possession of a process.

Read this as the practical chapter of the week's argument. If the age of reading is over, the exam is one of the last rooms where a person is still asked to produce a page without a model in the tab. Leavis wanted "Yes, but — ." Hunter wants a hand that has to keep moving. Read the Atlantic. This briefing is the assignment: the blue book is not nostalgia. It is a technology for making a mind visible.
Hunter's attic of old booklets is not cute. It is a claim that a career can still be read in handwriting. Abstraction in Modern Art, an A; Neurobiology, a B-minus. The pressure to sculpt a semester into a shape is the pedagogy. A laptop exam can be more accessible, more legible, kinder to a hand that cramps. He knows. He still wants the cramp, because the cramp is where a thought that was not pre-formed has to appear. Princeton's honour code died of a technology that made the honour unenforceable. The blue book's return can be read as reaction. Hunter reads it as a recovery of a human activity: trusting a mind to discover unknown capabilities. That sentence would be sentimental if the rest of the essay were not so concrete — the second booklet, the margin at the buzzer, the Morrison line on the inside cover. Read him after Horowitch. She says the age of reading is over. He is running a small counter-age for ninety minutes at a time.

articles.title: Textual Deviants
articles.summary: 伊金重访法国理论的美国来世：德里达他们不是虚无主义者；今天的文化战争，包括聊天机器人，仍是那场细读的遗产。
articles.briefing:
Emily Eakin's Harper's essay is about a set of names that once organised American English departments and now organise culture-war talking points: Derrida, Althusser, Barthes, Deleuze, Guattari, Lacan, and Paul de Man at Yale. What was everyone so worked up about? The piece's useful answer is not a primer. It is a history of use. In the United States, theory became a way to expose contradictions about gender, race, and class in almost any cultural object. François Cusset called it the American invention of French theory. Professors who had studied metaphor acquired the armature of a crusade. The sociologists of the present rarely admit that current fights — the death of truth, the nature of scientific knowledge, the collapse of a gender binary, the rights in authorless chatbot content, whether reason and justice still make sense as universals — are in part the afterlife of those postwar philosophers.

Eakin's correction matters because the cartoon is easy. The Frenchmen were not nihilists. They did not say reality is an illusion or that truth does not exist. They said language has real and mostly invisible effects, that intention and meaning often fail to coincide, that a close reading can show how a text works as ideology. They wanted readers to be wary consumers of signs. That discipline is almost the opposite of a feed, and almost the opposite of a model that will generate a fluent page without having meant anything. The chatbot is in the essay because it is the latest object that makes the old questions loud. Who is the author. What is a reading. What counts as a text when the text has no one behind it.

This is the third AI piece because the week's AI problem is not only a tool in a clinic. It is a change in what a sentence is. Lenharo measures skill loss. Hunter wants handwriting. Eakin wants you to remember that American intellectual life already lived through a panic about language, and that the panic produced methods — close reading, suspicion, the refusal of the obvious — that a postliterate, post-authorial public will need or will trash. Leavis, earlier in the issue, thought literature made life present. Theory thought literature made power visible. Both require a reader who will stay with a page. Horowitch says that reader is leaving.

Do not ask this briefing for a tour of Glas. Ask it for the stance. The Frenchmen were enlisted; the enlistment changed them; the conflicts of 2026 still speak their dialect, including when the speaker has never read them. Read Harper's. The argument is already in the room: if you want to fight about AI and truth, you are already inside a reading of reading.
De Man is the name that still makes the American story ugly: theory, Yale, a wartime journalism that surfaced later and stained the whole import. Eakin does not need that scandal to make her point, and a digest should not use it as a shortcut. The point is the method. Close reading as a way of not being a naive consumer of signs was a postwar export that the United States turned into a profession and then into a politics. When a chatbot produces a fluent page, the naive consumer is back, with better grammar. The culture war that blames "French theory" for every unravelling is, on Eakin's account, already speaking theory's language: there is no innocent text, including the one that says there is. A reader of this issue who has just come from Snow and Leavis will recognise a later round of the same temperament fight. Exactness versus meaning, now with a model in the middle. Read Harper's for the names and the uses. This briefing is only the afterlife.

articles.title: New psychedelic clinics treat rare post-trip harms
articles.summary: 约翰霍普金斯开了美国第一家专治迷幻药远期伤害的诊所：狂躁、精神病，以及挥之不去的视雪。
articles.briefing:
Dawn Fallik's Scientific American report is the unfashionable paragraph in a boom. States are legalising. The federal mood has warmed. A majority of Americans, in a recent survey, support medical psychedelic use. Psilocybin and MDMA have shown promise for PTSD and treatment-resistant depression. The drugs also trigger mania and bipolar illness in people with no such history, and they can leave rare, lasting perceptual damage. Last year Johns Hopkins opened the Clinic for Post-Psychedelic Difficulties, the first American clinic built to study and treat those long tails. Emory is expected to open another. Berlin has had an outpatient centre since 2017; Tomislav Majić sees 150 to 200 patients a year, including from abroad. Baltimore saw ten in its first year, limited to in-person or in-state telehealth.

Azin Bekhrad, who co-founded the Hopkins clinic, splits the patients. Some become manic or psychotic after a trip, sometimes with other drugs or alcohol. About half have hallucinogen persisting perception disorder: not a flashback only, but visual snow, halos, geometric shapes that do not leave. Symptoms often fade in a year. Majić has seen people suffer more than twenty years because they did not know a clinic existed. Treatment, developed from late-1990s case studies and now in larger trials, is typically antidepressants and antiseizure drugs; nearly a third recover fully within a year. Prevalence is foggy. Recreational use means harms go unreported. A web survey put HPPD around 4.2 percent of users. A 2024 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis found that the four percent with serious problems also had preexisting neuropsychiatric disorders. Majić thinks the numbers are undercounts, in part because researchers still fear that reporting serious harm will shut the field as it was shut in the late 1960s.

Michael Silver, at Berkeley's psychedelic centre, was surprised such clinics exist and notes that we do not build centres for the adverse events of most other drugs. He believes the experiences are often powerfully positive and that the main risks are psychological, a function of set and setting. Majić wants a non-ideological view: not toxic, not addictive, not without risk. Fallik's reporting was supported in part by the Pulitzer Center. The piece's discipline is to hold the boom and the clinic in one frame.

This issue's health cluster is about what we do with bodies after the story gets complicated: a trip that does not end, a corpse that needs a face, a man who wants a chemical back. Read Scientific American. This briefing is here so the renaissance does not erase the people who did not come back clean.
The stigma Majić describes is a research-policy loop. The 1960s shutdown taught a generation that talking about harm could end the work. The present boom teaches a generation that talking about harm could end the brand. A clinic with ten patients is not a crisis statistic. It is a place that makes the rare case countable. HPPD will never be the poster for legalisation, which is why it needs a door with a name on it. Silver's surprise — that we do not build such doors for other drugs — cuts both ways. Either psychedelics are being held to a stranger standard, or their advocates have been unusually unwilling to fund the unglamorous follow-up. Fallik's piece does not pick. It reports both rooms. A health column in a week about attention can use that double vision. The trip is sold as a way to see. The clinic is for people who cannot stop seeing. Read Scientific American, then keep both sentences. Bekhrad wants a network of providers who can talk about hard cases. That sentence is the opposite of a movement slogan. Networks are how rare harms become treatable instead of legendary. If the boom is real, the network will have more than ten patients. If the boom is mostly marketing, the clinic will remain a small, necessary embarrassment. Either outcome is information.

articles.title: A Dying Art
articles.summary: 塞姆利去芝加哥看殡葬修复大赛：火化率 63%，修复术正在变成一门没人再学的手艺。
articles.briefing:
John Semley's Harper's feature opens in a Chicago convention hall: eight undertakers, three hours, a decomposing head that is not a head. Post Mortem Restorative Cosmetics, founded by a Hollywood effects man who worked Blue Velvet and Deep Space Nine, casts silicone skulls at $855, grey, smashed, a patch of skull showing. The inaugural Restorative Art Technical Showcase is the NFDA convention's highlight. Anthony Saldivar, fifty, army infantry, Afghanistan and two Iraq tours, used to decompress with Fangoria and a Tom Savini school. He left Hollywood, did mortuary science in Texas, then Savini in reverse: instead of making the living look dead, he makes the dead look like someone a family can stand to see. "Sheepdog for the dead," he says. Time is always the biggest enemy.

The art is dying for reasons that are not mystical. Cremation passed burial about a decade ago and is at 63.4 percent, headed for 82.3 by 2045. Perhaps forty percent of cremations are direct: furnace, no casket, no embalming, no face. Explanations pile up: religious attendance at 34 percent, phones full of living photographs, environmental talk that ignores the quarter-ton of carbon a cremation releases. The most cited reason is cost. A traditional funeral averages about $8,300. Direct cremation can be $795. Jessica Mitford's 1963 American Way of Death is the ghost at the feast: Yorick sprayed, sliced, pickled, rouged into a Beautiful Memory Picture. Her book forced price lists. It did not make Americans rich enough to want the picture. Private equity — Carriage, Hillenbrand, SCI — wants a body restored in thirty minutes or a closed lid. Schools teach less. Lawsuits chill. Karl Wenzel, a judge, says the art of embalming itself is almost becoming lost.

Mitford thought the psychotherapeutic rationale was death-denying. The death-acceptance movement, Caitlin Doughty among them, wants unprocessed corpses and natural burial, and has become its own consumer category; human composting can run to $7,000. Semley stays with the people at the tables, putting hair on a silicone wound while the industry decides they are optional. Restorative art once expanded the client pool: after Crandall's demisurgery, almost no corpse was too damaged for an open casket. Prefabricated noses and eyeballs had a market. Now the skill is cosmetics over a small abrasion, and the showcase is a last public demonstration that the skill exists.

Personhood at the end of life was last issue's doulas. This issue's version is a face. A culture that will not look at a body still wants the option, and will not pay for the training. Read Harper's for Saldivar, the lab coat, Mitford's sarcasm, the trophy. This briefing will not describe a real head. It will say what kind of article you are opening: a craft feature about a labour the market is deleting while families still cry over a photograph.
Saldivar's hexagonal business card, the Slayer beard, the precise elocution: Semley is writing a person, not a thesis about America and death. The thesis arrives anyway. A country that photographs the living constantly has less use for a last look, and a country that cannot afford $8,300 will take the $795 furnace. Mitford's sarcasm still lands, and it does not settle the question of whether a family that wants a face should be able to find someone who can make one. Corporate thirty-minute caps answer no. The showcase answers, for a weekend, yes. Restorative art began as an expansion of who could be viewed. It is ending as a specialty the chains do not need. That arc is the opposite of a wellness story. It is a labour story. Read Harper's for the convention floor and for Mitford's Yorick. This briefing will not tell you how to mourn. It will say the skill of making a dead face presentable is being priced out of the culture that still uses the phrase "memory picture."

articles.title: The light narrows
articles.summary: 布朗在父亲死后去比柔术，血检说他的睾酮像十二岁；化学外挂能赢，光会在 choke 里收窄。
articles.briefing:
Wes Brown's memoir is a health essay that refuses the wellness voice. In the months after his father's death he signs up for Brazilian jiu-jitsu competitions, nameless men in sports halls, energy drinks and blocked toilets, five-minute rounds, points for takedowns and pins. Eight days after the death he meets a bigger, higher-ranked opponent. The loss is cellular. Another man's weight is a shadow play of the grief. He is swept, driven to the mat. The title's last image — the light narrowing as a choke lands — is not a metaphor he saves for the end. It is the sport's ordinary apocalypse, and then it becomes a medical one.

A blood test tells him he has the testosterone of a twelve-year-old boy. The adverts arrive: TRT as a cheat code, five symptoms, he has all of them. Hemingway used boxing as evidence of manhood. Brown has been using the mat the same way. It was not even about winning. The brush with defeat was where he felt most alive, until the number. Men on the clinics' websites describe their previous lives as shadows. The Substance is in the essay because the film's rule — old self and new self are one — is the rule a hormone protocol breaks. Synthetic testosterone by mail. Shrunken balls, more cojones. Black-market peptides, why the hell not. The opponent you meet next time on Smoothcomp may be yourself, remade.

The piece will not give you a doctor's pamphlet, and this briefing will not either. It will keep the question Brown actually asks. What kind of strength was he chasing. The father's death sent him to the mat. The mat sent him to a lab. The lab offers a chemical that will change the match and the body that enters it. Low testosterone is a real endocrine fact. The market around it is a story about male fear, grief, and the wish to not be the man who is drowning in someone else's life force. A university reader who has been trained to hear "TRT" as either bro-science or liberation needs the essay's refusal of both. Brown is not a spokesman. He is a man who can feel the choke and the advert in the same week.

Read this last if you have read Horowitch. She says we have lost the long form. Brown's long form is a body: a death, a sport, a number, a temptation. The light narrows in a gym and in a culture that would rather ship a vial than sit with a loss. Read Aeon when you have a sitting. The original has the locker room, the gum shield, the night beside Becki. This briefing is the wager: strength that arrives by post is still a question, not an answer.
The locker room is the essay's other clinic. Nervous men, a disabled toilet, a gum shield, a bracket that writes your name next to a stranger's. Grief makes the choreography too intimate: coconut oil, detergent, someone else's vitality as a tide. Brown is not offering jiu-jitsu as therapy. He is offering it as a place where a body can still lose on purpose. The blood test changes the meaning of the loss. If the defeat was hormonal, the vial looks like justice. If the defeat was a father, the vial looks like a dodge. The essay holds both without a verdict, which is why it belongs in a health column rather than a gym advertisement. TRT is a real treatment for a real deficiency. It is also a market that has learned to speak the language of a twelve-year-old's number to a grieving adult. Read Aeon for the match and the night he cannot sleep. The light narrows either way. The question is what you call the dark.
